atmosphereSnippets: The roar of the crowd is deafening here at Ortona, a real motorsport cathedral in the heart of Italy. You can feel the passion radiating from the grandstands today.
Look at the sea of flags waving! The Tifosi are out in full force to support their drivers and teams at this iconic Italian circuit.
The setting sun casts a golden glow across the Ortona circuit. A picture-perfect day for racing on this challenging West configuration.
There's a palpable buzz in the air, Crofty. The shorter, more intense West layout always delivers close racing and dramatic moments.
From the paddock to the grandstands, the energy is electric. This 1.8km layout demands precision and bravery, and the fans know it.
The aroma of Italian cuisine mixes with the scent of burning rubber – a truly unique sensory experience only found here at Ortona.
The hills surrounding Ortona provide a stunning backdrop to the circuit, creating a natural amphitheater for the fans.
The passion of the Italian fans is unmatched. They live and breathe motorsport, and their support is a huge boost for the drivers.
You can see the influence of classic Italian design in the circuit layout, a blend of high-speed sections and tight, technical corners.
The atmosphere is building as we approach the start. The drivers will be feeling the weight of expectation from the passionate Tifosi.
historicalReferences: Who can forget Riccardo Patrese's stunning victory here in 1985, holding off a charging Senna in the final laps?
This track has seen its fair share of drama over the years. In 2003, Michael Schumacher secured his sixth World Championship here after a tense battle with Kimi Räikkönen.
The 'Ortona Miracle' of 1996, when Olivier Panis took his only F1 victory in the Ligier, after starting 14th in treacherous conditions.
The circuit has been modified over the years, but the spirit of the old Ortona remains, especially on this classic West layout.
Many great drivers have graced this circuit, from Ascari and Fangio to Prost and Hamilton. Their names are etched into Ortona's history.
In 1970, Jochen Rindt won a thrilling race at Ortona, but tragically lost his life just weeks later at Monza.
Ortona has always been a happy hunting ground for Ferrari. The Tifosi expect nothing less than a victory on home soil.
The 1994 race was a controversial one, with Schumacher taking the win after a collision with Damon Hill. The debate still rages on today.
This West layout, though shorter, has seen some incredible last-lap overtakes into the final corner – a testament to its design.
Remember Gerhard Berger's dominant win in 1988? He led from start to finish, a masterclass of driving around Ortona.

strategyPoints: Tire wear is always a concern at Ortona, especially on this abrasive West layout. Managing the tires will be key to a successful race.
The pit window is relatively short here, meaning teams will need to be efficient with their stops to avoid losing valuable time.
Fuel consumption will be a factor on this 1.8km circuit. Drivers will need to balance performance with fuel conservation.
With only 5 turns, track position is crucial. Overtaking can be difficult, so a good qualifying performance is essential.
The shorter West configuration favors cars with strong acceleration and braking performance.
A well-timed safety car could shake things up, but teams will need to be ready to react quickly.
The low-speed corners of the West layout put a premium on mechanical grip. Teams will be optimizing their setups accordingly.
With such a short lap, traffic management will be crucial during qualifying. Finding a clean lap will be a challenge.
weatherCommentary: The Mediterranean climate can be unpredictable. A sudden downpour could turn this race on its head.
The wind can often pick up in the afternoon, affecting the car's stability, particularly through the high-speed sections.
The temperature is rising, which will impact tire degradation. Teams will be monitoring the situation closely.
The sun is beating down on the track, creating challenging conditions for the drivers and their cars.
With the mountains nearby, we sometimes see localized showers that can catch teams off guard.
